content: Valley Forge General Hospital, located in Phoenixville, Pennsylvania, was a former military hospital near both Philadelphia and Valley Forge. It holds the distinction of being the only United States Army General Hospital named after a specific place. The hospital was constructed in 1942 and officially opened on Washington's Birthday in 1943 to provide care for wounded soldiers during World War II. It eventually became the largest military hospital in the United States, accommodating over 3,000 patients and consisting of more than 100 separate buildings. The hospital's design featured primarily two-story buildings connected by corridors, with long ramps facilitating the movement of wheelchairs and gurneys. The exterior of the hospital was constructed with red brick, giving it the appearance of a New England college campus, while the interior was made entirely of wood, typical of military buildings from that era. The layout of the hospital was complex, with a maze of corridors that often caused newly assigned personnel to lose their way. The hospital ultimately ceased operations in 1974 and was officially closed in 1975. The site is now occupied by Valley Forge Christian College. Valley Forge General Hospital played a significant role in popular culture and medical advancements. It served as the setting for the 1951 film Bright Victory, which highlighted the rehabilitation of blinded soldiers. The hospital was a global leader in the rehabilitation of blinded personnel, pioneering many techniques in this field. One of its notable medical innovations was the development of the acrylic eye, created by one of the hospital's dentists, which remains in use today. The hospital's Department of Psychiatry and Neurology was at the forefront of psychiatric treatment, introducing new medications and developing innovative therapeutic techniques. The medical staff, including physicians, nurses, and neuropsychiatric technicians, successfully treated tens of thousands of patients, returning them to active duty at a rate significantly higher than that of most civilian hospitals. Among the notable individuals who served at the hospital was the actor Gene Wilder, who worked as a neuropsychiatric technician there in the late 1950s. In the late 1960s, Valley Forge General Hospital became the site of an advanced Clinical Specialist training program for military medics (MOS 91C). This rigorous nine-month program required candidates to have at least two years of prior experience as medics and a minimum of two years remaining in their enlistment after completing the training. Graduates of this program were eligible to challenge the Registered Nurse (RN) licensing boards after leaving the Army. The hospital lacked on-site married housing for its personnel, leading many staff members to rent homes in nearby communities such as Phoenixville, Norristown, and Pottstown. Many personnel also became active in local organizations and volunteer fire departments. Given the hospital's wooden interior and interconnected buildings, all enlisted personnel were required to undergo basic fire training, which included operating fire hoses, driving fire trucks, and using various fire equipment. After the release of the film Bright Victory, all hospital personnel were required to watch the movie. In the late 1960s, the hospital underwent extensive renovations costing millions of dollars. This decision was considered a significant loss to both the military and the local community.
